newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ election steals the show from c/account data.
newsitem.headline: NZ election steals the show from c/account data.

text.p: The significance of New Zealand's June quarter balance of payments data was undermined by the looming general election, economists said on Friday.
They said the figures were slightly worse than the market expected, due mainly to a fall in the invisibles balance.

Earlier, Statistics New Zealand said the June quarter current account deficit was NZ$836 million, compared with a March quarter deficit of NZ$47 million and economists' forecasts of a $550 million deficit.
The current account deficit for the year to June was NZ$3.66 billion, unchanged from the March year and slightly worse than economists' expectations ($3.41 billion).
Bankers Trust chief economist David Plank said while the data were "not overly important just one day before the election", they were mildly negative for the currency.
Bancorp executive director Roger Kerr was more emphatic.
"The relevance of today's release, one day from the most significant political event this decade, is non-existent," he wrote in a commentary.
New Zealanders go to the polls on Saturday for the country's first general election under a proportional voting system, and recent polls show a change of government could be in store.

SBC Warburg economist Robin Clements said the invisibles balance, which fell NZ$1.6 million in the June quarter and $4.4 billion over the year, explained why the overall deficit was worse than he had expected.
ASB economist Anthony Byett said while it was good to see merchandise exports at a record high, imports had slowed.

"That is the sort of thing we had to see to really arrest the growing deficit, but there's still that large deficit...There is still the large invisibles balance, which is probably going to take some time to rectify," he said.

Finance Minister Bill Birch said the fall in the invisibles balance was due in part to the usual seasonal winter decline in inbound tourism and a fall in migrant funds inflows, due to lower immigration.
Bancorp's Kerr said the September quarter should see a continuation of the trend shown by the June quarter results.

"The exchange rate we know has continued to stay high and the domestic economy has not shown any great signs of a turnaround. Based on this we expect the deficit to worsen, but only by $100-$200 million," he said.
